title: Electrical power and exhaust safety
audience: Trainees and workers on the pressure cleaning (all heights) track, working under supervision, who set up electric or petrol-powered equipment on site.
learningOutcomes: Inspect the power supply, leads and connections for an electric pressure cleaner before use.
Explain why a petrol-engine pressure cleaner must not run in an enclosed space.
Identify electrical work that is outside the scope of a cleaning worker and refer it correctly.

instruction.heading: Electrical hazards around water
instruction.body: An electric pressure cleaner combines electricity with water, which increases the risk of electric shock. Before use, check the power point, the lead and the plug. The power point should be in good condition and suitable for outdoor use. The lead should be undamaged, of a suitable rating, and free of joins. Keep the lead off wet ground and away from the spray. If the power point or lead is damaged, wet or unfamiliar, do not use it, and report it. Where the site has residual current protection, confirm it is working as the manufacturer directs before connecting the equipment.

instruction.heading: Testing and maintaining electrical equipment
instruction.body: AS/NZS 3760 is the reference standard named for electrical equipment inspection. Follow the employer's test-and-tag or inspection schedule for the equipment, and remove from service any item that fails inspection, shows damage, or has been wet inside its housing.

instruction.heading: Petrol engines and exhaust
instruction.body: Never run the engine in a garage, shed, enclosed courtyard, under a carport roof or any room with limited airflow. Place the machine outdoors, upwind of people, air intakes and windows, and keep the exhaust directed away from the work area. If a worker feels dizzy, has a headache or feels unwell while the machine is running, stop the machine, move to fresh air and seek medical advice.

instruction.heading: Fuel, refuelling and storage
instruction.body: Stop the engine and allow it to cool before refuelling. Keep fuel in an approved container, away from the engine, sources of ignition and occupied areas. Do not carry fuel in the cabin of a vehicle used for transport where the employer's rules forbid it.

instruction.heading: Fixed wiring and outdoor power points
instruction.body: A cleaning worker does not repair, alter or install fixed wiring, outdoor power points or switchboards. If a fault is suspected, stop using that power point, make it safe by not using it, and refer it to a licensed electrician or the site controller. In New South Wales, electrical wiring work includes repairing and altering, so repairs to fixed wiring need a licence or certificate (NSW Government licensing page, last updated 23 June 2026).

instruction.heading: Equipment modification and attachments
instruction.body: Do not modify the electrical or engine parts of the equipment, bypass a safety device, or fit an attachment that the manufacturer has not approved. The WorkSafe Victoria alert says attachments and changes need written approval from the manufacturer or a competent person (reviewed 11 May 2023). Report any part that seems faulty and remove the equipment from service until a competent person has checked it.

instruction.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instruction.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant an electrical licence, a contractor licence or any authority to repair, alter or install electrical equipment or wiring. Repairs to fixed wiring are licensed work in New South Wales (NSW Government licensing page, last updated 23 June 2026).

procedure: Inspect the power point, plug and lead, and confirm the lead has no damage, joins or moisture.
Confirm the power point is suitable for outdoor use and that any protective device is working as the manufacturer directs.
Keep the lead off wet ground and clear of the spray path.
Confirm the equipment's inspection or test record is current under the employer's schedule.
For a petrol-engine machine, place it outdoors, upwind of people and air intakes, with the exhaust directed away from the work area.
Stop the engine and allow it to cool before refuelling, and store fuel in an approved container away from ignition.
Stop and report if a fault, damage, moisture or a symptom of exhaust exposure appears.
Record the inspection, the position of the machine and any fault found.

workedExamples.situation: A worker needs to run a petrol pressure cleaner to clean a carport. The carport is roofed and enclosed on three sides.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the machine run there, and what is the alternative?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. An enclosed or partly enclosed carport has limited airflow, so exhaust gas can build up. Move the machine outdoors, upwind of people and windows, and direct the exhaust away from the work area. If the job can only be done under cover, the supervisor must re-plan it before work starts.

workedExamples.situation: The power point outside a house is warm to the touch, and the plug fits loosely when the worker connects the electric cleaner.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not use the power point. A warm point and a loose plug are signs of a fault. Disconnect nothing that is live without the proper process, do not attempt a repair, and tell the customer or site controller. Refer the outlet to a licensed electrician. Record the observation and the decision.

equipmentAndPpe: Inspection checklist for the power point, plug, lead and any protective device
Current inspection or test record for the equipment under the employer's schedule
Approved fuel container and a clear area for refuelling
Eye protection, gloves and hearing protection as the job pack specifies

commonErrors.error: Running a petrol engine in a garage or enclosed carport.
commonErrors.prevention: Place the machine outdoors and upwind, and direct the exhaust away from people and the work area.

commonErrors.error: Using a damaged lead or a warm power point because the job is urgent.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, make the point or lead unusable, and refer it to a licensed electrician.

commonErrors.error: Repairing a fault in the equipment or the wiring.
commonErrors.prevention: Refer the fault to the manufacturer, a competent person or a licensed electrician.
Stop the engine and allow it to cool before refuelling.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Carbon monoxide: petrol-engine exhaust must not run in an enclosed or poorly ventilated space, and exposure symptoms mean leaving the area and seeking medical advice.
Electrical equipment inspection: AS/NZS 3760 is the reference standard named.
Equipment modification: attachments and changes need written approval from the manufacturer or a competent person (WorkSafe Victoria alert, reviewed 11 May 2023).

Licence notice: This lesson does not grant an electrical licence, contractor licence or authority to repair or install electrical equipment or wiring. Repairing fixed wiring is licensed work in New South Wales (NSW Government licensing page, last updated 23 June 2026).

qualityStandard: The power point, plug and lead are inspected and found undamaged before use.
A petrol-engine machine is never run in an enclosed space.
Faulty equipment or wiring is removed from use and referred, and no repair is attempted by the worker.
The inspection record is current for the equipment in use.
documentationEvidence: Pre-use inspection of the power point, plug and lead
Equipment test or inspection record with the date
Record of the machine's position and exhaust direction for petrol-engine work
Fault report and referral record for any electrical or engine defect
summary: Water and electricity together raise the shock risk, so inspect the power point and lead before use.
Never run a petrol-engine pressure cleaner in an enclosed space.
Refer electrical faults to a licensed electrician rather than repairing them.
This lesson grants no electrical licence or authority to repair equipment or wiring.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must a petrol-engine pressure cleaner not run in an enclosed carport?
options: Exhaust gas, including carbon monoxide, can build up in an enclosed space
It is too noisy for the neighbours and everyone on the whole street
The engine needs open sky to start and run properly each time it is used
The pressure drops under a roof and the jet loses its force at once

knowledgeChecks.question: A power point is warm and the plug fits loosely. What is the correct action?
options: Use it quickly, because the job is urgent and the client is waiting
Stop using the point and refer it to a licensed electrician
Tape the plug and continue with the job as planned
Use a longer lead from the same point, since it is safer

knowledgeChecks.question: Under what condition may a worker repair an electrical fault on the cleaner?
options: Whenever the worker is confident in their own skill and training
When the customer agrees to the repair being done on the day
Never, unless the manufacturer or a competent person has authorised it
Whenever the fault is small and can be fixed quickly on the job

knowledgeChecks.question: Before refuelling a petrol-engine machine, what must happen?
options: Refuel while the engine is running
Refuel after the job is finished
Refuel inside the enclosed space
Stop the engine and allow it to cool

knowledgeChecks.question: Does this lesson grant an electrical licence?
options: No, the lesson grants no electrical licence or authority to repair wiring
Yes, for outdoor power points on the site where it is wet and damp today
Yes, once the quiz is passed by the worker and the employer signs off
Yes, if the employer agrees to it in writing for the job today

officialReferences.title: Carbon monoxide exposure in enclosed spaces
officialReferences.covers: SafeWork NSW guidance on carbon monoxide. Work in enclosed or restricted spaces poses a higher exposure risk, and use of combustion-engine plant should be minimised where ventilation is poor. Lists short-term symptoms including dizziness, nausea, impaired judgement and unconsciousness, and long-term symptoms including headaches. Names generators and petrol-powered pumps; does not name petrol-engine pressure cleaners. Publisher: SafeWork NSW (NSW Government).
